topic.examWeightHint: Question 1 of the B1 Foundation paper in three of the four series read: a labelled cell diagram with three structures to name [1] each, a table of functions [1] each and two plant-only structures [2] — 8 marks in Summer 2025, 6 in March 2026, 4 in Summer 2024 (a bacterial cell that year). Microscopy is examined in Unit 7 Biology Booklet B Question 1 instead: apparatus names [1] each, a magnification calculation [2] and a cell:nucleus ratio [1].
mustMemorise: Animal cell: nucleus (contains chromosomes), cytoplasm, cell membrane, nuclear membrane, mitochondria
Cell membrane controls the substances entering and leaving the cell; the cell wall provides support
Plant extras: cellulose cell wall, large permanent vacuole (cell sap), chloroplasts (chlorophyll, photosynthesis)
Bacterial cell: cell wall without cellulose, no nucleus, plasmids present
Total magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens

sheet.howExamined: B1 is 1 hour: 60 marks at Foundation, 70 at Higher, calculator allowed. Cells open the Foundation paper in most series — Summer 2025 Q1 (8 marks: name three structures [3], functions of three more [3], two plant-only structures [2]), March 2026 Q1 (a plant cell with a description-matching part), Summer 2024 Q1 (a bacterial cell). Microscopy sits in Unit 7 Biology Booklet B Q1 (35 marks in 30 minutes): name the apparatus [1] each, calculate a magnification [2] with a working line, and give a ratio from a printed scale [1]. Schemes here are pure point-for-point [1] lines with a tight accept list, and the listing rule bites: a right name beside a wrong one scores nothing.
traps: Cell wall written for cell membrane, or the other way round — the commonest loss on B1 F Q1 (Summer 2025)
Chloroplast offered for cytoplasm, or named from a diagram that does not show it (Summer 2025, Summer 2024, March 2026)
The function of the vacuole left blank or given as 'controls what enters' (Summer 2025 B1 F Q1(a)(ii))
'Provides support' missed for the cell wall (March 2026 B1 F Q1(b))
Plasmid not recalled when the diagram is bacterial (Summer 2024 B1 F Q1(b)); 'no cell wall' written instead of 'no cellulose'
Coverslip, slide and eyepiece lens not named (Summer 2025 U7 Booklet B Q1(b)(i), (c)(i))
Magnification found by subtracting one lens from the total instead of dividing (Summer 2025 U7 Booklet B Q1(c)(ii))
Cell:nucleus ratio written the wrong way round (Summer 2025 U7 Booklet B Q1(a)(iii))

noteBlocks.lede: A cell is the smallest unit a living thing is built from, and every part inside it has a job. Animal and plant cells share most of those parts; plant cells add three more. A light microscope and a drop of iodine make them visible on a slide.
can: Name each cell structure and say what it does.
Tell a bacterial cell from a plant or animal cell.
Calculate total magnification and order cell, tissue, organ, organ system.

noteBlocks.md: Everything alive is built from cells, and most of them are far too small to see. Under a school microscope an onion skin turns into rows of brick-shaped boxes, each with a wall, a nucleus and a jelly-like inside. Plant cells carry three parts that animal cells do not.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which structure controls what enters and leaves a cell?
noteBlocks.explain: The membrane is the gate. The wall is outside it and only gives support — and it is not there at all in an animal cell.

noteBlocks.md:
Work outwards, and say what each one **does**, because the function is what the mark is for.
**Cell membrane** — controls the substances entering and leaving the cell.
**Cytoplasm** — where the cell's chemical reactions happen.
**Nucleus** — contains the chromosomes, so it controls the cell.
**Nuclear membrane** — the membrane around the nucleus.
**Mitochondria** — where the reactions of respiration occur.

noteBlocks.title: Why the wall and the membrane are not the same job
noteBlocks.md: The **cell membrane** is a thin living layer that **chooses** what crosses it, which is why every cell has one. The **cellulose cell wall** outside it is a stiff scaffold that lets everything through and only holds its shape.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which part of a cell is where its chemical reactions happen?
noteBlocks.explain: The cytoplasm. The nucleus controls the cell; mitochondria do respiration.

noteBlocks.title: The three plant extras, with their jobs
noteBlocks.md:
**Cellulose cell wall** — a stiff layer outside the cell membrane that provides **support**. Bacteria and fungi have walls too, but not made of cellulose.
**Large permanent vacuole** — a liquid-filled space holding **cell sap**; it keeps the cell firm and helps it hold its shape.
**Chloroplasts** — contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which structure holds cell sap and helps a plant cell keep its shape?
noteBlocks.answer: vacuole | large permanent vacuole | the vacuole
noteBlocks.explain: The large permanent vacuole. 'Stores water' is usually accepted, but 'support' or 'keeps the cell firm' is the safer answer because it is the function CCEA prints.

noteBlocks.caption: Onion epidermis stained with iodine, seen down a light microscope with an eyepiece scale across it.
noteBlocks.prompt: Name two structures you can see here that an animal cell would not have, and say why no chloroplasts are visible even though this is a plant.

noteBlocks.md: The onion is a storage bulb underground, so its cells make no chlorophyll — **no chloroplasts**, even though every other plant feature is there. That is exactly the trap CCEA set in March 2026: they asked which structure was *not* in the onion-cell diagram.

A **bacterial cell** is the odd one out. It has a cell wall, but not a cellulose one. It has **no nucleus** — its DNA sits loose in the cytoplasm as a single circle — and it carries small extra rings of DNA called **plasmids**. Three facts, and CCEA has asked for all three.

noteBlocks.prompt: A diagram shows a bacterial cell. Which structure is present?
noteBlocks.explain: Plasmids are the bacterial giveaway. There is no nucleus and no chloroplast, so neither can be named from the diagram.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2025 B1 Foundation Q1, March 2026 B1 Foundation Q1, Summer 2024 B1 Foundation Q1
noteBlocks.md: In Summer 2025 many named the three structures but **swapped cell wall and cell membrane**, and several wrote chloroplast where cytoplasm was wanted; the function of the vacuole was the part most often left blank. In March 2026 candidates missed that the **cell wall provides support**, and fewer could say the chloroplast was the structure absent from an onion cell. In Summer 2024 the diagram was bacterial: nucleus was named easily, **plasmid** was not.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which structure is missing from an onion cell?
noteBlocks.explain: Chloroplasts. An onion bulb grows underground and makes no chlorophyll.

noteBlocks.md:
To make a **temporary slide**: peel a thin piece of tissue, lay it flat on a **slide**, add one drop of **iodine** solution as a stain so the structures are easier to see, then lower a **coverslip** at an angle so no air bubbles are trapped. Start on the lowest-power objective and focus with the **focusing wheel**.
**Total magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens.** It is a multiplication both ways: if the total is ×100 and the objective is ×10, the eyepiece is 100 ÷ 10 = ×10.

noteBlocks.prompt: A ×10 eyepiece is used with a ×40 objective. The total magnification is ×
noteBlocks.explain: 10 × 40 = 400. The answer is a magnification, so it has no unit — write ×400, never 400 mm.

noteBlocks.md: A **specialised** cell is one with adaptations for a particular job. Many of the same kind together make a **tissue**; different tissues working together make an **organ**; organs working together make an **organ system**. The order is the answer to a whole class of one-mark questions, and it is the frame for the rest of B1.

noteBlocks.prompt: Put these in order, smallest first.
noteBlocks.explain: Cells build tissues, tissues build organs, organs build systems. One step at a time, never skipping the tissue.

noteBlocks.md:
Name the parts of an **animal** and a **plant cell** and give each function.
Say what the **cell wall**, **vacuole** and **chloroplasts** do.
Spot a **bacterial cell** by its **plasmids**.

Cells almost always open the paper: three lettered structures named, a table of functions, then two structures a plant cell has and an animal cell does not. Microscopy is examined in Booklet B instead, where the magnification working line earns its own mark. Stuck: name what you can, and write the calculation out in full.

steps.decision: Write the relationship before any numbers. In Booklet B the working line is its own marking point, so a bare answer risks half the marks even when it is right.

The unknown is one of the two factors, so divide the total by the lens you were given. This is the exact spot where Summer 2025 candidates subtracted instead: 600 − 15 would give 585, which is not a lens that exists.

options: Divide, because the two magnifications multiply together
Subtract, because one lens is taken off the total
whyMenu.explain: Magnification is a multiplying factor. To undo a multiplication you divide.

steps.decision: Write the two numbers in the order the question names them — cell first, then nucleus. Reversing them is the single most common loss on this item.
Simplest form means divide both sides by the highest common factor, here 12. A ratio has no unit, so nothing is written after the numbers.

items.stem: Which structure is found in a plant cell but never in an animal cell?
items.skill: Separate the plant-only structures from the shared ones

options.feedback: Cell wall, large permanent vacuole and chloroplasts are the three plant extras. Everything else on the list is in both.
Every cell has a membrane, including animal cells; the plant cell has a wall as well, outside it. The membrane controls what enters and leaves, the wall gives support.
Mitochondria are in both. They are where the reactions of respiration occur, and animals respire too.
Both cells have a nucleus with a membrane around it. Look for wall, vacuole, chloroplast.

items.stem: What is the function of the large permanent vacuole?
items.skill: State the function of the vacuole in CCEA's words

options.text: It contains cell sap and helps support the cell
options.feedback: That is the wording the scheme wants: cell sap, and support or maintaining the cell's shape.

options.text: It controls what enters and leaves the cell
options.feedback: That is the cell membrane. The vacuole is a liquid-filled space inside the cytoplasm, not a barrier at the edge.
That is the chloroplast, and it is green because it holds chlorophyll. The vacuole holds cell sap.
Chromosomes are in the nucleus. Summer 2025 examiners reported the vacuole as the function candidates most often could not give.

items.stem: A diagram of a bacterial cell is shown in the exam. Which of these could you name from it?
items.skill: Recall what a bacterial cell does and does not contain

options.feedback: Plasmids are the small rings of extra DNA that only bacteria have on this specification. Summer 2024: most candidates missed this one.
A bacterial cell has no nucleus. Its DNA is a single loop lying free in the cytoplasm, which is the point of the comparison question.
No chloroplast. Naming a structure that is not on the diagram earns nothing, however well it is spelled.
There is a cell wall, but it is not made of cellulose — the spec says so in as many words, and 'cellulose' turns a right answer into a wrong one.

items.stem: Cells are viewed at a total magnification of ×100 using a ×10 objective lens. What is the magnification of the eyepiece lens?

options.feedback: 100 ÷ 10 = 10. The two lenses multiply, so to find one of them you divide the total by the other.
100 − 10 = 90 is a subtraction, and the examiners named it in Summer 2025 as the common error here. Magnifications multiply, so undo them by dividing.
That multiplies the total by the objective. The total is already the product of the two lenses, so divide.
Adding the two gives no meaningful quantity. Total = eyepiece × objective, so eyepiece = total ÷ objective.

parts.stem:
A student is given a piece of rhubarb stalk, a light microscope and the usual laboratory apparatus.
Describe how the student would prepare a temporary slide of the rhubarb epidermis and use the microscope to see its cells clearly.
Your written communication is assessed in this question, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: peel or cut a thin piece of epidermis so light can pass through it
place it flat on a (microscope) slide
add a drop of water or iodine solution
the stain makes the cell structures easier to see
lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid trapping air bubbles
place the slide on the stage and start with the lowest-power objective lens
focus using the focusing wheel, then change to a higher-power objective

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Write it as ordered sentences with capital letters and full stops — the quality of the writing decides where inside the band your mark lands.
Name the apparatus: slide, coverslip, stage, objective lens. Vague words such as 'glass' and 'the lens' are not credited.
parts.workedSolution: Peel a thin strip of epidermis from the rhubarb stalk so light can pass through it. Lay it flat on a microscope slide and add one drop of iodine solution, which stains the cells and makes their structures easier to see. Lower a coverslip onto it at an angle so that no air bubbles are trapped. Place the slide on the stage and select the lowest-power objective lens. Turn the focusing wheel until the cells are sharp, then move to a higher-power objective and focus again.

commonErrors.feedback: Booklet B pays for the names: slide, coverslip, stage, objective lens, eyepiece lens. A description that never names the apparatus is capped in Band C.

findTheMistake.stem:
Órlaith is asked: 'Cells were viewed at a total magnification of ×400. The eyepiece lens is ×10. Calculate the magnification of the objective lens. Show your working out. [2]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The relationship on line 1 is right, and it is a multiplication. To find one factor from the product you divide, so the second line should be 400 ÷ 10. Subtracting gives ×390, and no objective lens is anywhere near that.
findTheMistake.feedback: The first marking point is earned: the relationship was written before the numbers, which is what Booklet B pays for. The second is lost at line 2. A quick sense check catches it — school objective lenses are ×4, ×10 and ×40, so an answer of ×390 cannot be right.
